title: Kernel-aware speculative router with statistical acceptance and staged fallback
creator: Ethan Brooks
description:
Background: We need a runtime mechanism that opportunistically routes prefill+decode requests to lighter-weight candidate models (or quantized kernels) to reduce tail latency and GPU cost while preserving output quality. Past tickets (ENG-13521, ENG-14012) prototyped routing and acceptance thresholds; this task builds a production-grade 'kernel-aware speculative router' that considers kernel compatibility, attention optimization fingerprints, and sequence-length distributions when selecting candidates.

Goals: 
- Implement a router that is aware of available kernel implementations (FP16, int8, 4-bit kernels, fused attention variants) and picks candidate execution paths that maximize throughput under latency SLOs.
- Define and emit a compact statistical acceptance metric (per-model acceptance_histogram + moving acceptance_rate) for speculative decoders to decide when to accept candidate outputs without full decode.
- Provide a staged fallback policy (local fast-fallback -> cross-model fallback -> full decode) and an operator-configurable grace window for acceptance.
- Instrument end-to-end telemetry (per-request kernel chosen, estimate of compute saved, acceptance outcome, quality regression tag) for A/B rollouts and automatic rollback on regressions.

Success criteria (measurable):
- 10-25% average token-inference cost reduction for chat-heavy workloads in the Canary pool.
- 95th percentile latency improvement of at least 30ms for short-turn queries (<64 tokens) in Canary.
- No more than 0.5% relative regression on selected quality evals across rollout (prompt-set tied to model/tenant).

Design (high level):
1) Kernel capability registry: runtime maintains a per-host catalog of kernel implementations (name, quantization, optimized_attention_flags, max_seq_len, memory_budget_estimate). Registry exposes a simple scoring interface: score(candidate_kernel, request_profile) -> numeric.
2) Candidate selection: given a prefill request, router builds 2-3 candidate execution plans ranked by expected tail latency and cost. Plans can be: same-model-light-kernel (quantized), smaller-model-prefill (shorter KV footprint), or two-stage prefill (fast prefix-only prefill then hand off to full model).
3) Acceptance metric: each candidate emits an acceptance_score for its early-decode output. We maintain per-model moving-window acceptance_histogram (buckets: 0-0.1, 0.1-0.5, 0.5-0.9, 0.9-1.0) and driving acceptance_rate. Router uses a configurable acceptance_threshold plus an adaptive grace factor based on recent regression signals.
4) Staged fallback: if candidate accept fails, fallback proceeds through: (a) local alt-kernel (same host, compatible kernel), (b) remote compatible instance with full-decoder, (c) queue for full decode on dedicated capacity. All transitions attach trace IDs and cost estimates.

Telemetry & Signals:
- Emit: kernel_name, kernel_hash, selection_score, acceptance_score, acceptance_bucket, fallback_reason, latency_ms_prefill, latency_ms_decode, tokens_saved_estimate, quality_flag (none/low/medium/high).
- Aggregate: per-tenant acceptance_rate, quality_regression_count, cost_savings_by_model.

Rollout plan:
- Dev branch + unit tests (1 week).
- Internal perf canary on non-production cluster with synthetic chat traffic (2 weeks): measure cost & latency signals; evaluate quality against prompt-set small_eval_2025.
- Gradual rollout: 5% traffic -> 20% -> 50% with automated checks on acceptance_rate and quality_regression_count. Automatic rollback if regressions exceed thresholds.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- How aggressive should the acceptance_threshold be initially? Conservative thresholds protect quality but reduce gains. Proposal: start at 0.85 acceptance_score with a +10% grace window for cache-friendly tenants.
- Kernel compatibility graph complexity: do we enforce strict binary compatibility or allow best-effort (with runtime fallbacks)? For release-1 keep conservative (only explicitly declared compatible kernels).
- Where to store acceptance_histogram? In-memory sliding window per-runtime is fastest but loses cross-host visibility. Proposal: keep local moving-window + periodic aggregation to central metric service for analysis.

Risks:
- Silent quality regressions if acceptance metric miscalibrates for certain tenant prompts. Mitigation: tie to quality evals and create per-tenant prompt set where possible.
- Increased complexity in routing logic could add CPU overhead; need microbenchmarks to ensure router cost < saved decode cost.
